marrow__ANAT_CH58_Q001.takeaway: Obturator internus tendon exits the pelvis through the lesser sciatic foramen only; it does not traverse both foramina.
marrow__ANAT_CH58_Q001.displayText:
Obturator internus tendon exits the pelvis through the lesser sciatic foramen only; it does not traverse both foramina.

The tendon of the obturator internus muscle passes only through the lesser sciatic foramen.

Structures passing through both the greater and lesser sciatic foramina are the pudendal nerve, internal pudendal vessels, and nerve to obturator internus.
emphasis: Obturator internus tendon exits the pelvis through the lesser sciatic foramen only; it does not traverse both foramina

rationales.a: The pudendal nerve exits through the greater foramen and re-enters through the lesser foramen around the sacrospinous ligament.
rationales.c: The nerve to obturator internus exits through the greater foramen and then curves through the lesser foramen to reach the muscle.
rationales.d: Internal pudendal vessels follow the pudendal nerve through both foramina.

marrow__ANAT_CH58_Q002.takeaway: Linea semilunaris marks the lateral rectus sheath and is formed by the aponeuroses of the abdominal wall, not solely external oblique.
marrow__ANAT_CH58_Q002.displayText:
Linea semilunaris marks the lateral rectus sheath and is formed by the aponeuroses of the abdominal wall, not solely external oblique.

Linea semilunaris is derived from the aponeurosis of the internal oblique muscle.

Pectineal ligament, inguinal ligament and lacunar ligament are derived from the external oblique aponeurosis.
emphasis: Linea semilunaris marks the lateral rectus sheath and is formed by the aponeuroses of the abdominal wall, not solely external oblique

rationales.a: The pectineal ligament is the medial continuation of the inguinal ligament, which is formed by external-oblique aponeurosis.
rationales.b: The inguinal ligament is the rolled inferior margin of external-oblique aponeurosis.
rationales.c: The lacunar ligament is a medial reflection of the inguinal ligament and therefore derives from external-oblique aponeurosis.

marrow__ANAT_CH58_Q003.takeaway: The femoral triangle floor is formed mainly by iliopsoas laterally and pectineus/adductor longus medially; psoas minor is not a floor muscle.
marrow__ANAT_CH58_Q003.displayText:
The femoral triangle floor is formed mainly by iliopsoas laterally and pectineus/adductor longus medially; psoas minor is not a floor muscle.

Psoas major forms the floor of the femoral triangle, not psoas minor.

The femoral triangle is an intermuscular space in the anteromedial aspect of the thigh. Its lateral boundary is the medial margin of sartorius, its medial boundary the medial margin of adductor longus, and its floor from lateral to medial is formed by iliacus, psoas major, pectineus and adductor longus.
emphasis: The femoral triangle floor is formed mainly by iliopsoas laterally and pectineus/adductor longus medially; psoas minor is not a floor muscle

rationales.a: Iliacus contributes with psoas major to the lateral part of the triangle floor.
rationales.c: Pectineus forms the medial floor of the femoral triangle.
rationales.d: Adductor longus contributes to the medial floor and also forms the medial boundary.

audit.tablesAndFigures: Retained by unchanged native structuredExplanation and source figure metadata.

marrow__ANAT_CH58_Q004.takeaway: The medial edge of sartorius forms the lateral boundary of the femoral triangle; adductor longus forms its medial boundary.
marrow__ANAT_CH58_Q004.displayText:
The medial edge of sartorius forms the lateral boundary of the femoral triangle; adductor longus forms its medial boundary.

The lateral boundary of the femoral triangle is formed by the medial margin of the sartorius. Its medial boundary is formed by the medial margin of adductor longus.
emphasis: The medial edge of sartorius forms the lateral boundary of the femoral triangle; adductor longus forms its medial boundary

rationales.a: Adductor longus is on the medial side of the triangle, not the lateral boundary.
rationales.b: The medial margin of adductor longus is the medial boundary, rather than the lateral side.
rationales.c: The lateral edge of sartorius faces away from the triangle; its medial margin bounds the space.

marrow__ANAT_CH58_Q005.takeaway: The femoral sheath contains the femoral vessels and medial femoral canal lymphatics; the femoral artery lies lateral to the vein.
marrow__ANAT_CH58_Q005.displayText:
The femoral sheath contains the femoral vessels and medial femoral canal lymphatics; the femoral artery lies lateral to the vein.

The lymphatic vessels lie medial to the femoral vein and are likely to be injured in this case.

The femoral sheath is the funnel-shaped prolongation of the fascia containing femoral vessels. It is divided into three compartments by intervening septa: lateral compartment contains femoral artery, intermediate compartment contains femoral vein, and the medial compartment (femoral canal) contains lymphatic vessels, areolar tissue and the lymph node of Cloquet.

The empty space in the femoral canal allows distension of the adjacent femoral vein with increased venous return or increased intra-abdominal pressure.
emphasis: The femoral sheath contains the femoral vessels and medial femoral canal lymphatics; the femoral artery lies lateral to the vein

rationales.b: Femoral artery is lateral to the femoral vein within the sheath, not medial to it.
rationales.c: The femoral nerve lies lateral to the sheath and is not contained within it.
rationales.d: The genitofemoral nerve runs on psoas and its femoral branch enters the thigh lateral to the sheath, not its medial compartment.

marrow__ANAT_CH58_Q006.takeaway: The injured femoral nerve lies lateral to the femoral artery and outside the femoral sheath.
marrow__ANAT_CH58_Q006.displayText:
The injured femoral nerve lies lateral to the femoral artery and outside the femoral sheath.

The nerve injured is the femoral nerve. The femoral nerve is not a content of the femoral sheath.

The femoral nerve lies lateral to the femoral artery. The source contrasts this with sciatic nerve injury, which can occur after misplaced intramuscular gluteal injection and may cause sensory loss over the outer ankle/heel and foot drop.
emphasis: The injured femoral nerve lies lateral to the femoral artery and outside the femoral sheath

rationales.a: The femoral nerve lies lateral, not medial, to the femoral artery.
rationales.c: The described anterior-thigh pain pattern implicates femoral nerve, not the sciatic nerve of posterior thigh/leg.
rationales.d: Femoral nerve fibers arise from posterior divisions of L2–L4, not anterior divisions.

marrow__ANAT_CH58_Q007.takeaway: The pectineal (Cooper) ligament forms the posterior boundary of the femoral ring traversed by a femoral hernia.
marrow__ANAT_CH58_Q007.displayText:
The pectineal (Cooper) ligament forms the posterior boundary of the femoral ring traversed by a femoral hernia.

A femoral hernia passes through the femoral ring proximally. The posterior border of the femoral ring is the pectineal ligament.

Relations of the femoral ring: anteriorly inguinal ligament; posteriorly pectineal ligament, superior pubic ramus and pectineus; medially lacunar ligament; laterally femoral vein.
emphasis: The pectineal (Cooper) ligament forms the posterior boundary of the femoral ring traversed by a femoral hernia

rationales.a: The inguinal ligament forms the anterior border of the femoral ring.
rationales.b: The lacunar ligament forms its medial border.
rationales.d: The femoral vein lies lateral to the ring and is a structure at risk, not its posterior boundary.

marrow__ANAT_CH58_Q008.takeaway: Adductor magnus forms the adductor hiatus through which the femoral vessels pass into the popliteal fossa.
marrow__ANAT_CH58_Q008.displayText:
Adductor magnus forms the adductor hiatus through which the femoral vessels pass into the popliteal fossa.

In this scenario, the femoral vessels are injured at the adductor hiatus. The adductor hiatus is an opening in the tendon of adductor magnus; hence the muscle likely involved is adductor magnus.

Clinical relevance: the adductor part of adductor magnus attaches to the distal femur. Distal femur fractures may cause femoral artery injury and impair blood supply to the lower leg.
emphasis: Adductor magnus forms the adductor hiatus through which the femoral vessels pass into the popliteal fossa

rationales.a: Adductor longus does not form the hiatus; the vessels pierce the distal adductor magnus tendon.
rationales.b: Adductor brevis is proximal and does not contain the hiatus for femoral vessels.
rationales.d: Sartorius roofs the adductor canal, but does not form the hiatus.

marrow__ANAT_CH58_Q009.takeaway: The adductor (Hunter) canal lies deep to sartorius in the medial thigh.
marrow__ANAT_CH58_Q009.displayText:
The adductor (Hunter) canal lies deep to sartorius in the medial thigh.

Hunter's canal lies beneath the sartorius muscle. It is also called the subsartorial or adductor canal and is a triangular intermuscular tunnel occupying the lower two-thirds of the medial thigh.
emphasis: The adductor (Hunter) canal lies deep to sartorius in the medial thigh

rationales.a: Vastus medialis is a lateral wall of the canal, not its roof.
rationales.b: Adductor longus contributes to the posterior wall proximally, but sartorius overlies the canal.
rationales.d: Adductor magnus forms part of the posterior wall, not the muscle immediately overlying the canal.

marrow__ANAT_CH58_Q010.takeaway: The adductor canal contains the femoral artery and vein, saphenous nerve and nerve to vastus medialis; the femoral nerve proper ends above it.
marrow__ANAT_CH58_Q010.displayText:
The adductor canal contains the femoral artery and vein, saphenous nerve and nerve to vastus medialis; the femoral nerve proper ends above it.

The femoral nerve is least likely to be encountered while giving an adductor canal block. The adductor canal does not contain the femoral nerve.

Contents of the adductor canal include the saphenous nerve, nerve to vastus medialis, femoral artery, descending genicular artery, femoral vein and deep lymphatic vessels.
emphasis: The adductor canal contains the femoral artery and vein, saphenous nerve and nerve to vastus medialis; the femoral nerve proper ends above it

rationales.a: The saphenous nerve is a sensory branch that travels through the canal and is often targeted by the block.
rationales.b: The nerve to vastus medialis is a canal content and may be encountered.
rationales.d: The femoral artery is a major content of the canal and is the structure the block must avoid.

marrow__ANAT_CH58_Q011.takeaway: Within the adductor canal the saphenous nerve crosses anterior to the femoral artery toward the medial knee.
marrow__ANAT_CH58_Q011.displayText:
Within the adductor canal the saphenous nerve crosses anterior to the femoral artery toward the medial knee.

The saphenous nerve is anterior to the femoral artery in the adductor canal.
emphasis: Within the adductor canal the saphenous nerve crosses anterior to the femoral artery toward the medial knee

rationales.a: The nerve crosses anterior to the artery; it is not described as medial to the femoral vein.
rationales.b: The saphenous nerve is anterior, not posterior, to the femoral vessels in the canal.
rationales.d: The nerve passes anterior to the femoral artery, not behind it.

marrow__ANAT_CH58_Q012.takeaway: Biceps femoris forms the superolateral border of the popliteal fossa.
marrow__ANAT_CH58_Q012.displayText:
Biceps femoris forms the superolateral border of the popliteal fossa.

The surgeon should use the biceps femoris muscle for a superolateral popliteal-fossa flap because biceps femoris forms the superolateral border of the popliteal fossa.

The popliteal fossa is a diamond-shaped region posterior to the knee.
emphasis: Biceps femoris forms the superolateral border of the popliteal fossa

rationales.a: Semitendinosus forms part of the superomedial border.
rationales.b: Semimembranosus forms part of the superomedial border.
rationales.c: Medial gastrocnemius forms an inferomedial border, below the fossa.

marrow__ANAT_CH58_Q013.takeaway: The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve supplies anterolateral thigh skin and does not enter the popliteal fossa.
marrow__ANAT_CH58_Q013.displayText:
The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve supplies anterolateral thigh skin and does not enter the popliteal fossa.

The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is not a content of the popliteal fossa. It arises from the ventral rami of L2 and L3 and supplies the skin of the anterolateral thigh.

Contents of the popliteal fossa listed by the source include popliteal artery and branches; popliteal vein and tributaries; tibial nerve; common fibular (peroneal) nerve; short saphenous vein; posterior femoral cutaneous nerve; articular branch of obturator nerve; medial and lateral sural cutaneous nerves; lymph nodes; fat; and bursae.
emphasis: The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve supplies anterolateral thigh skin and does not enter the popliteal fossa

rationales.a: The posterior femoral cutaneous nerve descends into the gluteal fold and posterior thigh, reaching the fossa region.
rationales.b: An articular branch of obturator nerve can contribute to the knee joint and is included among fossa contents.
rationales.c: The lateral sural cutaneous nerve arises from the common fibular nerve in the fossa and supplies upper lateral leg skin.

marrow__ANAT_CH58_Q014.takeaway: The anterior pillar of the lateral longitudinal arch is formed by the fourth and fifth metatarsals.
marrow__ANAT_CH58_Q014.displayText:
The anterior pillar of the lateral longitudinal arch is formed by the fourth and fifth metatarsals.

The anterior pillar of the lateral longitudinal arch of the foot is formed by the 4th and 5th metatarsals.
emphasis: The anterior pillar of the lateral longitudinal arch is formed by the fourth and fifth metatarsals

rationales.a: These medial-arch bones form the anterior pillar of the medial, not lateral, arch.
rationales.c: The third metatarsal belongs with the medial/transverse support rather than the lateral arch’s anterior pillar.
rationales.d: This list includes the medial arch bones and omits the lateral pair of fourth and fifth metatarsals.
